title: JWT structure
short: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.
answer: Header has metadata, payload has claims, signature protects integrity/authenticity. Base64URL is not encryption.
interview: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.

title: Authentication vs authorization
short: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.
answer: Roles, scopes and policies are authorization mechanisms.
interview: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.

title: CSRF
short: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.
answer: It is especially relevant to cookie-based authentication. CORS is not a general CSRF defense.
interview: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.

title: Password storage
short: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.
answer: bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 are typical choices. Never store plaintext or reversibly encrypted passwords.
interview: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.

title: OAuth 2.0
short: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.
answer: Authorization Code with PKCE is common for user-facing apps. OpenID Connect adds identity.
code: Client -> Authorization Server -> Token -> Resource Server
interview: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.

title: CORS
short: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.
answer: It is browser-enforced; server-side authorization is still required.
interview: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.

title: Refresh token
short: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.
answer: Refresh tokens need stronger protection, rotation and revocation strategies.
interview: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.

title: RBAC
short: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.
answer: Roles map identities to authorities. Complex systems may need policies/permissions.
interview: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.

title: Service-to-service security
short: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.
answer: mTLS, OAuth2 client credentials or workload identity are common approaches.
interview: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.

title: REST API security checklist
short: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.
answer: Review broken access control, injection, token handling, request limits and dependency vulnerabilities.
interview: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.

title: Secure cloud backend
short: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.
answer: Prefer workload identities/roles over static keys and use layered network/application controls.
interview: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.

title: How does JWT authentication work?
short: On login, the server validates credentials and issues a signed JSON Web Token containing claims (user id, roles, expiry) and a signature. The client sends this token in the \Authorization: Bearer \ header on subsequent requests; the server
answer: On login, the server validates credentials and issues a signed JSON Web Token containing claims (user id, roles, expiry) and a signature. The client sends this token in the \Authorization: Bearer \ header on subsequent requests; the server verifies the signature and expiry (no database/session lookup needed) to authenticate the request, making JWT auth stateless and easy to scale horizontally.

title: Difference between authentication and authorization.
short: Authentication verifies who you are (validating credentials — login). Authorization determines what you're allowed to do once identified (checking permissions/roles against a requested resource or action). Authentication always happens firs
answer: Authentication verifies who you are (validating credentials — login). Authorization determines what you're allowed to do once identified (checking permissions/roles against a requested resource or action). Authentication always happens first; authorization decisions depend on its outcome.
interview: Authentication verifies who you are (validating credentials — login). title: Explain API Gateway authentication flow.

answer: The gateway sits in front of backend services and intercepts every incoming request, validating the presented credential (e.g. a JWT's signature and expiry, or introspecting an opaque token against an auth server) before forwarding the request — so individual downstream services can trust the request has already been authenticated, often just reading pre-validated identity/claims passed via headers rather than re-validating themselves.

title: Explain JWT validation flow.
short: The verifier decodes the token's header and payload, checks the signature against the issuer's public key (or shared secret) to confirm it hasn't been tampered with, checks standard claims like expiry (\exp\) and issuer (\iss\), and then tr
answer: The verifier decodes the token's header and payload, checks the signature against the issuer's public key (or shared secret) to confirm it hasn't been tampered with, checks standard claims like expiry (\exp\) and issuer (\iss\), and then trusts the claims inside (user id, roles) for authorization decisions — all without needing to call back to the issuing server for typical stateless JWT validation.

title: Explain OAuth2 authorization code flow.
short: The client redirects the user to the authorization server to log in and consent; the server redirects back to the client with a short-lived authorization code; the client's backend exchanges that code (plus its client secret) for an access
answer: The client redirects the user to the authorization server to log in and consent; the server redirects back to the client with a short-lived authorization code; the client's backend exchanges that code (plus its client secret) for an access token (and often a refresh token) via a direct server-to-server call — keeping the actual token exchange off the user's browser, which is why this flow is considered secure for server-side web apps.
